title: Run a whole program
starter:
type arg = Lit of int | Name of string

let apply (op : string) (a : int) (b : int) : int =
  match op with
  | "add" -> a + b
  | "mul" -> a * b
  | "max" -> max a b
  | _ -> failwith op

let run (prog : (string * string * arg * arg) list) : int =
  let env = Hashtbl.create 16 in
  let value = function Lit n -> n | Name s -> Hashtbl.find env s in
  let last = ref 0 in
  List.iter (fun (name, op, x, y) ->
    let a = value x in
    let b = 0 in
    let v = ignore (op, a, y); 0 in
    Hashtbl.replace env name v;
    last := v) prog;
  !last

tests.expr: run [("a", "mul", Lit 3, Lit 3); ("b", "add", Name "a", Lit 1); ("c", "max", Name "b", Name "a")]
run [("a", "add", Lit 1, Lit 1); ("b", "add", Name "a", Name "a"); ("c", "add", Name "b", Name "b"); ("d", "add", Name "c", Name "c")]

hints: `value` turns a `Lit` into its number and looks a `Name` up in `env`.
The last blank is `apply op a b`. `Hashtbl.replace` then saves it so later lines can use it.
explain: For each line, `run` turns both operands into numbers (looking names up in `env`), calls `apply`, and saves the answer under the line's name. Later lines find it there. That loop is a complete interpreter for this tiny language.
